title: The Binmen of Birmingham - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Alex Tabarrok uses Birmingham City Council's equal-pay-driven binmen dispute as a natural experiment showing the refuse-collection bonus was a compensating differential, not sexism: after the council deleted the premium in January 2025 the binmen struck for eighteen months, 17,000 tonnes of rubbish piled up, and the council ended up paying roughly triple its pre-strike outsourcing bill. He argues the UK Equality Act's comparator rules created a fiscal bomb that contributed to Birmingham's 2023 bankruptcy and that closing the contractor 'loophole' will push the problem up the supply chain.

themes.theme: Market wage revealed by natural experiment

insights.claim: Birmingham's post-strike outsourcing of refuse collection cost roughly triple its pre-strike outsourcing bill and more than it had been paying its own employees, empirically demonstrating the binmen's premium was the market price of the job rather than gender favoritism.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: When administrative pay-setting overrides market clearing for dirty/dangerous work, the cost resurfaces at a multiple through contractors — a template for modeling public-sector labor arbitrage costs.
insights.quote: The council hired an outside contractor to take over its rubbish collection and it now pays roughly triple its pre-strike outsourcing bill–more than it was paying its own employees.

insights.claim: Refuse collection, gardening and gravedigging command a wage premium because the work is filthy, heavy and outdoors — Adam Smith's 1776 compensating-differentials mechanism, not discrimination.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Compensating differentials are the first hypothesis to test before attributing occupational pay gaps to bias — the alternative explanation carries large fiscal consequences.
insights.quote: these jobs command a premium for exactly the reason Adam Smith gave in 1776 — compensating differentials
insights.locator: Why were the binmen given bonuses?

insights.claim: Female binpersons already exist at Birmingham and earn the same bonuses as their male counterparts, undercutting the sexism interpretation of the bonus structure since entry into the role was never restricted by gender.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Open-entry evidence is a cheap falsification test for pay-discrimination claims — the same argument the Next case turned on.
insights.quote: there is nothing stopping women from becoming “binpersons” and indeed there are female binpersons and they earn the same bonuses as their male counterparts
insights.locator: Well, note first that there is nothing

themes.theme: Equal-pay comparator math as a fiscal bomb

insights.claim: Birmingham employs roughly 400 binmen against about 6,000 women in comparable graded roles, so every extra pound paid to a binman implied about fifteen pounds owed across the comparator group.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: The 15x liability multiplier is the mechanism that turns a small occupational premium into an unpayable public balance-sheet obligation — screen other councils for similar headcount ratios.
insights.quote: The council employs roughly 400 binmen and something like 6,000 women in comparable graded roles. Every extra pound paid to a binman therefore implied about fifteen pounds owed to the cooks and cleaners.

insights.claim: The 2010 employment tribunal ruling that Birmingham City Council discriminated against thousands of female workers denied binmen-style bonuses contributed to the council going bankrupt in 2023.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Equal-pay litigation is a live contingent liability on UK local-authority balance sheets capable of triggering insolvency — a credit consideration for municipal exposure.
insights.quote: Here’s the problem, which contributed to Birmingham going bankrupt in 2023.

insights.claim: Because the council could not afford to raise 6,000 comparator workers to binman wages, it instead cut the binmen's pay — the arithmetically forced but economically destructive resolution of an equal-pay judgment.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Equal-pay enforcement in fiscally constrained employers levels down rather than up, predicting service disruption rather than wage gains.
insights.quote: The council simply didn’t have the money to pay everyone binman wages so they cut the binmen’s wages.
insights.locator: The council simply didn’t have the money

themes.theme: Strike, service collapse, and regulatory arbitrage

insights.claim: When Birmingham deleted the refuse premium in January 2025 the binmen struck and were still striking nearly eighteen months later, with 17,000 tonnes of rubbish accumulating and the city declaring a major incident.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Below-market administrative wage-setting for essential services produces multi-year service failure, not quiet savings — a concrete cost benchmark for similar disputes.
insights.quote: when Birmingham finally deleted the premium in January 2025, the binmen went on strike — and they are still on strike, nearly eighteen months later
insights.locator: But the market wage for collecting rubbish

insights.claim: Outsourcing worked as pure regulatory arbitrage because contractor binmen legally have a different employer than the council's female caregivers and the Equality Act's comparator rules stop at the employer's nexus.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Employer-boundary arbitrage is the predictable corporate response to comparator-based pay law — expect outsourcing volumes to rise wherever such rules bind.
insights.quote: Because the new binmen were contractors they legally had a different employer than the Council’s female caregivers and the Act’s comparator rules stop at the employer’s nexus.

insights.claim: UK government officials intend to close the contractor loophole by pushing equal-pay comparator requirements up the supply chain, extending the compliance burden to private contractors serving public bodies.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Outsourced-services providers to UK public bodies face a prospective new equal-pay compliance and liability channel — a margin risk for the facilities and outsourcing sector.
insights.quote: The government mandarins, of course, want to close the “loophole” adding yet another bureaucratic requirement to push the equal pay madness up the supply chain.
